title: Error Likely Interaction Review
excerpt: An error-likely interaction review is an analytical practice for identifying structurally error-prone interactions before or between usability test cycles. It classifies error mechanisms, consequences, and design requirements so design work can address foreseeable use error conditions.
metaDescription: Analytical review of structurally error-prone interactions, identifying error mechanisms, consequences, and design requirements before or between tests.
summary: Error-likely interaction review examines what an interaction requires from users and under which operating conditions that requirement is likely to produce error. The practice is used during Sandbox Experiments, Iterative System Building, and IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation contexts to identify error mechanisms, classify consequences, and define design requirements.
definition: An error-likely interaction review is an analytical practice that identifies interactions whose structure makes user error foreseeable, independently of whether the error has already appeared in observed usability testing.
keyFacts: The practice is not a usability test; it is an analytical review conducted before or between test cycles.
The central question is what the interaction requires of users and under what conditions that requirement will produce errors.
The review produces three outputs: error mechanism, error consequence, and design requirement.
Common error mechanisms include memory dependency, ambiguous state, insufficient confirmation friction, information absence, and single-channel communication.
The review is used during Sandbox Experiments on existing systems before design decisions are made.
The review is used during Iterative System Building on prototypes before implementation, particularly for critical tasks identified through task-criticality mapping.
In regulated medical device contexts, the review supports IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation and foreseeable misuse analysis.

The documented engagement evidence includes Kardion, deSoutter Medical / Zethon, Gexcon, Beissbarth, Typewise, Raymarine, Schone Airspace Group, Streetec, Egma, a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, and visioncheckout.
The practice supports design revision; the page does not claim that identified conditions prevented real-world errors.
bodyMarkdown:
## Summary

An error-likely interaction review is an analytical practice for identifying interactions whose structure makes user error foreseeable. It is conducted before or between usability test cycles, and it does not depend on a participant having already made the error in observed testing.

The review asks what the interaction requires of users and under what operating conditions that requirement will produce errors. A single confirmation step before an irreversible high-consequence action is error-likely even if no participant has clicked through it accidentally. A colour-only state indicator in variable lighting is error-likely before anyone misreads it in a test.

Creative Navy uses the review to identify structural conditions early enough for design work to address them before they become test evidence. The supportable claim is that error-likely conditions were identified analytically and designs were revised, not that a revised design prevented a real-world error.

## What the practice does

An error-likely interaction review separates observed errors from foreseeable error conditions. Usability testing can show what participants did in a particular study. Error-likely interaction review examines whether an interaction creates a structural pathway to error under plausible conditions of use.

The practice focuses on mechanisms rather than symptoms. A user clicking the wrong control is not the explanation by itself. The review asks whether the system state was ambiguous, whether the user had to remember information that was not visible, whether a high-consequence action had insufficient friction, whether required information was absent at the decision point, or whether a signal relied on a communication channel that can fail.

The result is a design requirement rather than a proposed screen solution. In regulated contexts, this requirement is documented and traceable to the identified hazard.

## Error mechanisms examined in the review

Memory-dependent interactions require users to recall information instead of recognising it from the interface. Examples include a calibration technician remembering which measurement sequence is current, a surgeon remembering which parameter a rotary knob is adjusting, or an officer remembering alert criteria for a goods category. These interactions become error-prone under time pressure or divided attention.

Ambiguous state at decision points occurs when the system state required for a correct decision is not clearly visible at the moment of decision. This includes configuration steps where prior values are not displayed, mode changes where the active mode is not indicated where its behaviour matters, and alarm states where the triggering condition is not shown alongside the alarm.

Insufficient confirmation friction occurs when irreversible or high-consequence actions can be completed with a single interaction step. The review identifies consequential actions and assesses whether confirmation friction is proportional to the consequence.

Information absence at decision points occurs when information needed for a correct decision exists somewhere in the system but is not surfaced where the decision is made. The user would make the right decision if the required context were available at that point.

Single-channel state communication occurs when a critical state indicator depends on one channel, such as colour, sound, text, or spatial position, and that channel may fail under operating conditions. In this mechanism, the channel failure is the proximate cause of the resulting error.

Foreseeable misuse patterns are uses of the system that were not intended but are predictable given the user population, operating conditions, and interface design. IEC 62366-1 requires foreseeable misuse to be identified explicitly, not only intended use.

## When Creative Navy applies error-likely interaction review

During Sandbox Experiments, Creative Navy applies error-likely interaction review to the existing system before design decisions are made. The output is an error profile that the design must address.

During Iterative System Building, Creative Navy applies the review to design prototypes before implementation. This is especially relevant for critical tasks identified through task-criticality mapping, because error likelihood is most consequential where task criticality is high.

In regulated medical device contexts, the review runs throughout the engagement as part of IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation. The review supports identification of foreseeable use errors and misuse, and it supports traceability between design decisions and identified hazards. Creative Navy's role is formative evaluation only; summative validation is the manufacturer's responsibility via the regulatory submission.

## Outputs of an error-likely interaction review

The first output is the error mechanism. The mechanism explains why the interaction produces errors. The mechanism may be memory dependency, ambiguous state, insufficient friction, information absence, single-channel communication, or another structural condition identified in the review.

The second output is the error consequence. The consequence is classified by reversibility and magnitude. A reversible low-consequence error requires a different design response from an irreversible safety-relevant error.

The third output is the design requirement. The requirement states what the design must achieve to reduce error likelihood to an acceptable level. It is not the same as a design solution. In regulated contexts, the requirement is formally documented and traceable to the identified hazard.

## Kardion MCS Controller evidence from IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation

In the Kardion MCS Controller engagement, the IEC 62366-1 formative evaluation process structured the error-likely interaction review. The review identified flow rate adjustment via rotary knob as a high-consequence action controlled through a single physical input. The error mechanism was insufficient confirmation friction, and the design requirement was a two-step confirmation pattern in which adjustment and confirmation are separate before the adjustment takes effect.

The Kardion review also addressed min and max flow value interpretation. A prior Emergo by UL formative study had identified user misreading of which value was minimum and which was maximum. The mechanism was visual ambiguity in the prior display, and the design requirement was that the primary flow visualisation make the hierarchy unambiguous without requiring interpretation.

The Kardion review also identified alarm state during mute as a foreseeable misuse condition. A user could silence an alarm and then forget it remained active. The mechanism was that alarm disappearance on mute removed the ongoing reminder. The design requirement was that muted alarms remain visually present at reduced prominence.

## deSoutter Medical and Zethon evidence from operating theatre conditions

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement, the operating theatre context defined the foreseeable use conditions and the foreseeable misuse profile. Activation state recognition was treated as the highest-risk interaction in the surgical workflow because a surgeon beginning the procedure with a mistaken understanding of instrument state could produce patient harm and instrument damage.

The activation-state mechanism was state communication relying on colour as the primary differentiator under variable lighting. The design requirement was redundant non-colour cues for the activation state indicator, using spatial, icon, and colour cues together.

Speed parameter adjustment during the procedure was also identified as error-likely because the interaction competed with primary surgical attention. The mechanism was the need to actively read the current parameter value while performing the procedure. The design requirement was that parameter adjustment be confirmable as a glance-check without interrupting workflow.

## Gexcon CFD simulation evidence from configuration setup review

In the Gexcon CFD simulation engagement, error-likely interaction review identified a configuration error pattern across the simulation setup workflow. Required input values were not clearly signalled as required before simulation initiation. Contradictory parameter combinations were not identified before run and were discoverable only in outputs that appeared valid.

The consequence in the Gexcon example was deferred. The error could produce a completed simulation with incorrect outputs rather than an immediate error message. The mechanism was information absence at the critical decision point, because the simulation setup screen did not surface which values were required, incomplete, or contradictory.

The design requirement was an interactive configuration warning architecture that surfaces incomplete and contradictory inputs before run.

## Beissbarth automotive calibration evidence from workshop observation

In the Beissbarth automotive calibration engagement, error-likely interactions were identified through contextual observation of calibration workflows across 5 workshops. Borderline tolerance measurement confirmation was one identified condition. Technicians encountering measurements in the borderline zone needed to distinguish clearly between a confirmed measurement and one requiring repetition.

The Beissbarth mechanism was insufficient visual distinction between tolerance zones. The design requirement was three-level measurement result communication, with confirmed, borderline, and out-of-range states receiving distinct visual treatment.

Calibration sequence state tracking was also identified as error-likely. Multi-step sequences required technicians to confirm that each step had been completed correctly before proceeding, but no persistent completion state was visible across the sequence. The mechanism was memory dependency, and the design requirement was a persistent sequence state display showing completed, current, and upcoming steps.

## Typewise AI keyboard evidence from domain learning

In the Typewise AI keyboard engagement, error-likely interaction review was part of the domain learning phase. Creative Navy installed and used the keyboard before beginning design work.

The review identified the adoption barrier as an error-likely condition at the product level. New users transitioning from the iOS native keyboard encountered an error rate substantially higher than experienced users because gestural patterns conflicted during the transition.

The mechanism was attentional competition between established motor habits and new interaction patterns. The design requirement was an adoption framework structured around Zone of Proximal Development, introducing new gestures within reach of existing competence to avoid transition-phase error accumulation.

## Raymarine evidence from a multi-screen walkthrough before build work

In the Raymarine engagement, a structured walkthrough before build work identified an error-likely condition because the walkthrough traversed screens rather than reviewing a single screen in isolation. On the fifth day of the first exploration sprint, a scenario walkthrough of routine calling, target browsing, incoming alerts, and a change of screen context identified physical control ambiguity and caused a dedicated control study to be inserted into the next sprint.

The conflict was that the lower encoder could be used to move between vessel targets in one concept, had already been assigned as the primary channel selector in the radio view, and would have had a third role in settings. If an alert interrupted an interaction, the next rotation could ambiguously select a vessel, change the tuned channel, or navigate a message.

The failure mode was structural. A visible object could move, so the action could appear accepted even when a mode error had occurred. The resolution principle was allocation-level prevention: where an input can silently change purpose, better labels added later cannot fully remove the ambiguity. Resolving the ambiguity before high-fidelity design protected subsequent flow work from rework.

## Schone Airspace Group evidence from review of Creative Navy design candidates

In Schone Airspace Group Mission Control, error-likely interaction review produced a catalogue of 18 findings in Creative Navy's own first design candidates. These were Creative Navy design candidates failing Creative Navy's own criteria, not findings about the client's existing product.

The findings were classified as 9 critical, 8 major, and 1 moderate. Each carried an identifier, a severity, the check it failed, the sprint in which it was revised, and the decision record that resolved it.

The nine critical findings form a taxonomy of interface ambiguity: wrong aircraft interpretation; stale telemetry displayed as current; acknowledgement shown as a completed flight state; partial offline map coverage appearing complete; measured telemetry mistaken for a manual check; command recipient disappearing when the operator switched to the camera workspace; no response treated as a rejected command; a cross-vehicle warning with no visible owner; inspecting another aircraft silently retargeting commands; and an uncertain link leaving return-to-launch looking available.

Severity in the Schone review recorded the consequence of interface ambiguity within the scripted task. It does not mean that corresponding aircraft incidents occurred.

## Streetec kntrl 2 evidence from vehicle-state constraints

In the Streetec kntrl 2 engagement, an interface action had a physical-damage consequence if the vehicle was in the wrong state. Before the full-deflate function is used, the wheels must be straight because the fenders can contact and break against the wheels.

The guard against adjustment in motion used three independent interlocks: accelerometer-detected movement, a calibrated speed signal with a user-set threshold, and a digital input such as the handbrake, configurable as active-high or active-low.

The engagement also included a separate minimum pressure rule. Minimum pressure per axle can never be overridden, including by manual adjustment, a preset, or the full-deflate function.

## Egma evidence from sandbox dependency analysis

In the Egma Order engagement, Creative Navy worked the existing configurator hands-on in a sandbox environment to establish hidden complexity and dependencies between configuration options. The review examined which choices foreclosed other choices and where a user could be left without a recoverable path.

The worked example from the support team involved an optometrist ordering reading lenses, completing half the steps, and then learning that lenses with the selected shape could not be produced. The patient did not want a different lens shape, the optometrist could not determine which parameters would allow the intended shape, and a support ticket was created instead of an order, with the support team placing the order on their behalf.

This Egma example is a support-team account of a failure mode. It is not evidence of a measured support-ticket volume, order-completion rate, or error-rate pattern. No post-launch figure is available for this page.

## Uncrewed systems command-and-control evidence from strike-control review

In the uncrewed systems command-and-control engagement, a catalogue of error-likely conditions was developed for one input device from the case against a permanently visible touchscreen strike control. A single touchscreen input was not treated as an adequate commitment gate for an irreversible action because touchscreens are vulnerable to accidental touches, rain and moisture, gloves, vibration and device movement, palm contact, selection of the wrong control under stress, and digitizer faults.

The review also identified false-affordance conditions. A strike control and an abort control placed symmetrically at opposite screen edges could imply that strike was mapped to an adjacent physical key when no such mapping existed. Toolbars running down both screen edges could also sit close enough to bezel keys to imply a non-existent button pairing.

The reusable rule from this review was that a visible and enabled control asserts that the action is always available, while availability may depend on connectivity, operating mode, and vehicle state that the control cannot see. A permanent control may create mode confusion and encourage repeated activation attempts, whereas a persistent status indicator communicates readiness without implying that activation will work.

The recommendations in this engagement were not validated. The hold duration and physical-control design require human-factors and system-safety testing that was not performed. This page does not claim that the design prevents accidental activation or operator error.

## visioncheckout evidence from the system being replaced

In the visioncheckout engagement, error-likely conditions were observed in the system being replaced. An empty glass on the tray could produce a charge alongside the drink it had held. Regular canteen users had learned to avoid this, and staff intervened at the public venue.

Guests taking food away sometimes left the lid on and did not know why recognition failed. The strongest identified condition was that one credential served simultaneously as identity, price level, and payment. An employee intending to pay by credit card could forget to present the employee card for the discount and pay more than they should.

Creative Navy placed the keycard-pays-immediately question into the flow diagram as an explicit callout. The counter-argument in the record was that double scanning risks bugs and guest frustration, and that 90–95% of guests pay by keycard.

These observations describe the system being replaced. The new designs were not tested with users, nothing had shipped, and no outcome of any kind is claimed here.

## Boundaries and limits

Error-likely interaction review does not replace usability testing. It identifies structurally error-prone conditions analytically, while usability testing observes what participants actually do under study conditions.

The practice does not prove that a specific real-world error occurred. For this page, the supportable claim is that Creative Navy identified conditions analytically and revised designs or design requirements in response.

The evidence is engagement-specific. Some examples are based on contextual observation, some on structured walkthrough, some on hands-on sandbox analysis, some on formative evaluation, and some on review of design candidates. These evidence bases should not be treated as interchangeable.

The Schone Airspace Group severity labels refer to consequences within scripted tasks and do not establish aircraft incidents. The Egma example is a support-team worked example and does not establish frequency. The visioncheckout examples describe the system being replaced and do not establish tested performance of new designs. The uncrewed systems command-and-control recommendations were not validated through human-factors or system-safety testing.

## Related pages

Error-likely interaction review draws on task-criticality mapping, because critical tasks define where error likelihood has the greatest consequence. It also draws on state and transition review, because state ambiguity is a primary error mechanism, and on cognitive load analysis, because high cognitive load under operating conditions predicts error likelihood.

Error-likely interaction review directly informs edge-case and degraded-mode analysis by identifying the interactions most likely to fail under non-nominal conditions. It also provides diagnostic evidence for error-reduction and recovery design.
